Thyroid dysfunction is one of the possible causes of TE. On the other hand, the link between thyroid disorder and TE is still being debated. The aim of this retrospective is to investigate the link between thyroid dysfunction and TE. This retrospective study included 500 female patients with TE who had thyroid function testing between January 2012 and December 2022. Patients were eligible if they had a confirmed TE diagnosis and thyroid function tests within 3 months of being diagnosed with TE. The thyroid function of the participants was classified as euthyroid, hypothyroidism, or hyperthyroidism. The severity of hair loss was determined using the severity of alopecia tool (SALT) score. The study included 500 TE females, 248 of whom were euthyroid, 150 had hypothyroidism, and 102 had hyperthyroidism. The hypothyroid group had a significantly higher mean SALT score than the other 2 groups. Furthermore, patients in the hypothyroid group had a higher proportion of severe hair loss. The mean SALT score did not differ significantly between groups with normal thyroid function and those with hyperthyroidism. A common cause of TE is thyroid dysfunction, particularly hypothyroidism. Patients with hypothyroidism have more severe hair loss than those with normal thyroid function or hyperthyroidism. To effectively identify and manage such cases, thyroid function testing should be included in the diagnostic workup of patients with TE. Hair follicles typically undergo a cyclic process of growth and replacement that lasts several years. Telogen effluvium (TE) is a hair loss condition characterized by an extended resting or telogen phase of the hair cycle.[6] While some hair shedding during this phase is normal, TE leads to excessive hair loss and a noticeable reduction in hair volume due to increased shedding of resting hair. Various factors can contribute to TE, including metabolic stress, hormonal changes, and medication use.[7] Thyroid hormones are well-established regulators of hair growth, and thyroid dysfunction can lead to various hair disorders, including telogen effluvium.[8,9] Telogen effluvium occurs when a higher number of hair follicles transition from the active growth (anagen) phase to the resting (telogen) phase. This extended resting phase results in excessive hair shedding, leading to the characteristic hair loss observed in TE.[10] The association between thyroid dysfunction and hair loss, including TE, has been extensively investigated. While some studies have suggested a link between the 2 conditions,[11,12] others have yielded conflicting results.[13,14] These inconsistencies may be attributed to limitations such as small sample sizes, lack of control groups, and retrospective study designs. Our primary objective was to investigate the link between thyroid dysfunction and TE by analyzing a cohort of 500 female patients with confirmed TE, who had thyroid function testing. Postpartum hair shedding is medically called **telogen effluvium**, and it is one of the most common hair-loss conditions after childbirth [N1-R1][N1-R2][N1-F1]. The simple explanation is that your body’s hormonal balance changes dramatically after giving birth, especially the sharp drop in estrogen, and that causes more hair to shift into the resting (telogen) phase of the hair growth cycle [N1-R4][N1-F1][N4-F2]. That is not a direct “hair loss” from damage, but rather a temporary redistribution of hair follicles, which then shed more than usual [N4-F2].

So, postpartum hair shedding is **usually normal and temporary** [N1-F1][N5-R2]. It is a well-known, expected part of the postpartum period, and most women are told it is nothing to be alarmed about [N1-F1].

The main difference between **normal shedding** and **abnormal shedding** is whether the loss is mild, short-lived, and expected, versus severe, persistent, or associated with other symptoms.

### Normal shedding:
- Occurs after childbirth and is usually mild
- Often peaks around 4 months after delivery and lasts up to 6–9 months [N5-R4][N5-R3]
- Hair gradually returns to normal thickness as hormone levels stabilize [N5-R2][N1-F1]
- Often resolves without specific treatment [N1-F1]

- May involve losing **more than four hairs when a doctor gently pulls on the scalp** [N4-R4]

- May not improve after several months or may continue for more than six months [N1-F1][N4-R2]
- May be associated with other symptoms such as fatigue, weight changes, or signs of thyroid dysfunction [N4-R1][N4-R3]

The evidence points to several key causes, with **hormonal changes** being the main driver.

The most important cause is the **postpartum drop in estrogen**, which causes more hair to enter the resting phase and shed [N1-R4][N1-F1][N4-F2]. This is why it is called **telogen effluvium**.

The evidence also points to stress and other postpartum changes as contributing factors [N3-R2][N3-R4]. This is consistent with the general understanding that stress can push more hair into the shedding phase [N3-R2][N3-R4].

The evidence also shows that **thyroid dysfunction** is a common cause of telogen effluvium, especially **hypothyroidism** [N4-R1][N4-R5][N4-F2]. There is **no cure** for postpartum hair loss itself, but there are things you can do to support your hair and reduce further damage [N2-R2][N1-F1]. The safest approach is to combine gentle hair care, good nutrition, and stress management with cautious use of natural remedies [N2-R2][N3-R4].

- Choose **gentle hair products and hairstyles** to avoid damage [N2-R2]

- Eat a **balanced diet** with essential nutrients [N3-R1]
- Focus on **good nutrition and stress management**, which are important for overall hair health [N3-R4]

- Avoid unproven or over-the-counter products that are not clearly supported by evidence [N6-R4]

- Do not assume that all supplements are safe or effective; evidence is thin for many postpartum hair remedies [N6-R4][N6-R2]

## 5) When to see a doctor or specialist

Postpartum hair shedding usually resolves on its own, but there are clear red flags that suggest an underlying condition and warrant medical attention.

### Red flags that suggest an underlying condition
- Severe or persistent hair loss
- Hair loss that does not improve after several months
- Hair loss that is diffuse and widespread rather than patchy
- Associated symptoms such as fatigue, weight changes, or other signs of thyroid dysfunction [N4-R1][N4-R3][N4-R2][N4-F2]

### Who to see
- First, talk to your **healthcare provider** if you are concerned [N1-F1][N4-R2]
- If thyroid dysfunction is suspected, **thyroid testing** should be part of the workup [N4-F2]
- If the hair loss is severe or persistent, a **dermatologist** may be the most appropriate specialist [N4-F2]

### Next steps if shedding is severe or persistent
- If the shedding continues for more than six months, see a provider [N1-F1]
- If you have other symptoms, get thyroid function testing and other relevant tests [N4-F2]
- If the hair loss does not improve, specialist evaluation is recommended [N4-R2][N4-F2]

## 6) Timeline, prognosis, and realistic expectations

### How long postpartum hair shedding usually lasts
Postpartum hair shedding typically begins within a few months of childbirth, peaks around 4 months after delivery, and lasts up to 6–9 months [N5-R4][N5-R3]. Most women see their hair return to normal thickness about 6–12 months after giving birth [N5-R2][N1-F1].

- Recovery is gradual, not immediate
- Hair density usually improves over time
- Most women find their hair returns to normal thickness within a **year or two** [N3-R4]
- In the meantime, gentle care, good nutrition, and stress management are recommended [N3-R4]

### When to expect a return to normal hair thickness
- Expect improvement within **6–12 months** [N5-R2][N1-F1]
- Some sources say hair can return to normal thickness within a **year or two** [N3-R4]
- The peak of shedding is around **4 months**, and the loss can last up to **9 months** [N5-R4][N5-R3]

## 7) Bottom line for a patient

If you are asking, “Can you fix postpartum hair shedding?” the short answer is:

- **Yes**, in the sense that it can be supported and managed with the right care.
- **No**, there is no single “magic pill” or instant fix for postpartum telogen effluvium [N2-R2][N1-F1].
- The best approach is to:
  - Understand that it is usually **normal and temporary** [N1-F1][N5-R2]
  - Use **gentle hair care, good nutrition, and stress management** [N2-R2][N3-R4]
  - Avoid unproven supplements and remedies that are not clearly supported by evidence [N6-R4][N6-R1]
  - See a healthcare provider if the shedding is **severe, persistent, or associated with other symptoms** [N1-F1][N4-F2][N4-R2]

In most cases, your hair will gradually return to normal thickness over several months to a year, and the biggest thing you can do is be patient and take care of your overall health [N5-R2][N3-R4].

# Postpartum hair shedding: what it is, why it happens, and what you can do

Postpartum hair shedding is medically called **telogen effluvium**, and it is one of the most common hair-loss conditions after childbirth [N1-R1][N1-R2][N1-F1]. The simple explanation is that your body’s hormonal balance changes dramatically after giving birth, especially the sharp drop in estrogen, and that causes more hair to shift into the resting (telogen) phase of the hair growth cycle [N1-R4][N1-F1][N4-F2]. That is not a direct “hair loss” from damage, but rather a temporary redistribution of hair follicles, which then shed more than usual [N4-F2].

So, postpartum hair shedding is **usually normal and temporary** [N1-F1][N5-R2]. It is a well-known, expected part of the postpartum period, and most women are told it is nothing to be alarmed about [N1-F1].

## 2) Normal vs abnormal shedding: how to tell them apart

The main difference between **normal shedding** and **abnormal shedding** is whether the loss is mild, short-lived, and expected, versus severe, persistent, or associated with other symptoms.

### Normal shedding:
- Occurs after childbirth and is usually mild
- Often peaks around 4 months after delivery and lasts up to 6–9 months [N5-R4][N5-R3]
- Hair gradually returns to normal thickness as hormone levels stabilize [N5-R2][N1-F1]
- Often resolves without specific treatment [N1-F1]

### Abnormal shedding:
- May involve losing **more than four hairs when a doctor gently pulls on the scalp** [N4-R4]
- May be **diffuse and widespread**, not localized or patchy [N4-F2]
- May not improve after several months or may continue for more than six months [N1-F1][N4-R2]
- May be associated with other symptoms such as fatigue, weight changes, or signs of thyroid dysfunction [N4-R1][N4-R3]

If you are losing hair severely, persistently, or in a way that feels out of the ordinary, that is a sign that the shedding may be more than just postpartum telogen effluvium [N4-F2][N1-F1].

## 3) Why postpartum hair shedding happens: the key causes

The evidence points to several key causes, with **hormonal changes** being the main driver.

### Hormone changes
The most important cause is the **postpartum drop in estrogen**, which causes more hair to enter the resting phase and shed [N1-R4][N1-F1][N4-F2]. This is why it is called **telogen effluvium**.

### Stress and other physiological changes
The evidence also points to stress and other postpartum changes as contributing factors [N3-R2][N3-R4]. This is consistent with the general understanding that stress can push more hair into the shedding phase [N3-R2][N3-R4].

### Secondary conditions that can mimic or worsen shedding
The evidence also shows that **thyroid dysfunction** is a common cause of telogen effluvium, especially **hypothyroidism** [N4-R1][N4-R5][N4-F2]. This means that if your shedding is severe or does not improve, it is important to consider thyroid function as part of the picture [N4-F2].

- Choose **gentle hair products and hairstyles** to avoid damage [N2-R2]

### Diet and lifestyle tips
- Eat a **balanced diet** with essential nutrients [N3-R1]
- Focus on **good nutrition and stress management**, which are important for overall hair health [N3-R4]

Postpartum hair shedding usually resolves on its own, but there are clear red flags that suggest an underlying condition and warrant medical attention.

- Severe or persistent hair loss
- Hair loss that does not improve after several months
- Hair loss that is diffuse and widespread rather than patchy
- Associated symptoms such as fatigue, weight changes, or other signs of thyroid dysfunction [N4-R1][N4-R3][N4-R2][N4-F2]

- First, talk to your **healthcare provider** if you are concerned [N1-F1][N4-R2]
- If thyroid dysfunction is suspected, **thyroid testing** should be part of the workup [N4-F2]
- If the hair loss is severe or persistent, a **dermatologist** may be the most appropriate specialist [N4-F2]

- If you have other symptoms, get thyroid function testing and other relevant tests [N4-F2]
- If the hair loss does not improve, specialist evaluation is recommended [N4-R2][N4-F2]

# Postpartum hair shedding: what it is, why it happens, and what you can do

## 1) What postpartum hair shedding really is

Postpartum hair shedding is medically called **telogen effluvium**, and it is one of the most common hair-loss conditions after childbirth [N1-R1][N1-R2][N1-F1]. The simple explanation is that your body’s hormonal balance changes dramatically after giving birth, especially the sharp drop in estrogen, and that causes more hair to shift into the resting (telogen) phase of the hair growth cycle [N1-R4][N1-F1][N4-F2]. That is not a direct “hair loss” from damage, but rather a temporary redistribution of hair follicles, which then shed more than usual [N4-F2].

So, postpartum hair shedding is **usually normal and temporary** [N1-F1][N5-R2]. It is a well-known, expected part of the postpartum period, and most women are told it is nothing to be alarmed about [N1-F1].

## 2) Normal vs abnormal shedding: how to tell them apart

The main difference between **normal shedding** and **abnormal shedding** is whether the loss is mild, short-lived, and expected, versus severe, persistent, or associated with other symptoms.

### Normal shedding:
- Occurs after childbirth and is usually mild
- Often peaks around 4 months after delivery and lasts up to 6–9 months [N5-R4][N5-R3]
- Hair gradually returns to normal thickness as hormone levels stabilize [N5-R2][N1-F1]
- Often resolves without specific treatment [N1-F1]

### Abnormal shedding:
- May involve losing **more than four hairs when a doctor gently pulls on the scalp** [N4-R4]
- May be **diffuse and widespread**, not localized or patchy [N4-F2]
- May not improve after several months or may continue for more than six months [N1-F1][N4-R2]
- May be associated with other symptoms such as fatigue, weight changes, or signs of thyroid dysfunction [N4-R1][N4-R3]

If you are losing hair severely, persistently, or in a way that feels out of the ordinary, that is a sign that the shedding may be more than just postpartum telogen effluvium [N4-F2][N1-F1].

## 3) Why postpartum hair shedding happens: the key causes

The evidence points to several key causes, with **hormonal changes** being the main driver.

### Hormone changes
The most important cause is the **postpartum drop in estrogen**, which causes more hair to enter the resting phase and shed [N1-R4][N1-F1][N4-F2]. This is why it is called **telogen effluvium**.

### Stress and other physiological changes
The evidence also points to stress and other postpartum changes as contributing factors [N3-R2][N3-R4]. This is consistent with the general understanding that stress can push more hair into the shedding phase [N3-R2][N3-R4].

### Secondary conditions that can mimic or worsen shedding
The evidence also shows that **thyroid dysfunction** is a common cause of telogen effluvium, especially **hypothyroidism** [N4-R1][N4-R5][N4-F2]. In one study, hypothyroid patients had more severe hair loss than those with normal thyroid function [N4-F2]. This means that if your shedding is severe or does not improve, it is important to consider thyroid function as part of the picture [N4-F2].

## 4) What you can do: safe, evidence-based remedies and treatments

There is **no cure** for postpartum hair loss itself, but there are things you can do to support your hair and reduce further damage [N2-R2][N1-F1]. The safest approach is to combine gentle hair care, good nutrition, and stress management with cautious use of natural remedies [N2-R2][N3-R4].

### Hair care practices that may help
- Use **gentle, sulfate-free shampoos** [N3-R1]
- Avoid harsh brushing, tight hairstyles, and heat styling [N2-R2]
- Consider **scalp massage with natural oils** such as coconut or argan oil, which may improve circulation and nourish hair roots [N3-R1][N2-R1]
- Choose **gentle hair products and hairstyles** to avoid damage [N2-R2]

### Diet and lifestyle tips
- Eat a **balanced diet** with essential nutrients [N3-R1]
- Focus on **good nutrition and stress management**, which are important for overall hair health [N3-R4]
- Get enough **sleep** and manage stress, since stress can worsen shedding [N3-R2][N3-R4]

### Supplements and vitamins
The evidence is more cautious on supplements. The search results say there is **little to no evidence that prenatal vitamins prevent postpartum hair loss** [N6-R4]. That means they are not a proven remedy, though they may support overall health. Other natural ingredients such as **rosemary oil, pumpkin seed oil, and melatonin extract** have been studied for hair growth, but the evidence for them is limited and should be used cautiously [N6-R2][N6-R1].

### What to avoid or be cautious about
- Avoid unproven or over-the-counter products that are not clearly supported by evidence [N6-R4]
- Be cautious about **essential oils and natural remedies**; while they may be used safely, they should be used with care and not relied on as a cure [N6-R1]
- Do not assume that all supplements are safe or effective; evidence is thin for many postpartum hair remedies [N6-R4][N6-R2]

## 5) When to see a doctor or specialist

Postpartum hair shedding usually resolves on its own, but there are clear red flags that suggest an underlying condition and warrant medical attention.

### Red flags that suggest an underlying condition
- Severe or persistent hair loss
- Hair loss that does not improve after several months
- Hair loss that is diffuse and widespread rather than patchy
- Associated symptoms such as fatigue, weight changes, or other signs of thyroid dysfunction [N4-R1][N4-R3][N4-R2][N4-F2]

### Who to see
- First, talk to your **healthcare provider** if you are concerned [N1-F1][N4-R2]

- If the hair loss is severe or persistent, a **dermatologist** may be the most appropriate specialist [N4-F2]

- If you have other symptoms, get thyroid function testing and other relevant tests [N4-F2]
- If the hair loss does not improve, specialist evaluation is recommended [N4-R2][N4-F2]

### How long postpartum hair shedding usually lasts
Postpartum hair shedding typically begins within a few months of childbirth, peaks around 4 months after delivery, and lasts up to 6–9 months [N5-R4][N5-R3]. Most women see their hair return to normal thickness about 6–12 months after giving birth [N5-R2][N1-F1].

# Postpartum hair shedding: what it is, why it happens, and what you can do

## 1) What postpartum hair shedding really is

Postpartum hair shedding is medically called **telogen effluvium**, and it is one of the most common hair-loss conditions after childbirth [N1-R1][N1-R2][N1-F1]. The simple explanation is that your body’s hormonal balance changes dramatically after giving birth, especially the sharp drop in estrogen, and that causes more hair to shift into the resting (telogen) phase of the hair growth cycle [N1-R4][N1-F1][N4-F2]. That is not a direct “hair loss” from damage, but rather a temporary redistribution of hair follicles, which then shed more than usual [N4-F2].

So, postpartum hair shedding is **usually normal and temporary** [N1-F1][N5-R2]. It is a well-known, expected part of the postpartum period, and most women are told it is nothing to be alarmed about [N1-F1].

## 2) Normal vs abnormal shedding: how to tell them apart

The main difference between **normal shedding** and **abnormal shedding** is whether the loss is mild, short-lived, and expected, versus severe, persistent, or associated with other symptoms.

### Normal shedding:
- Occurs after childbirth and is usually mild
- Often peaks around 4 months after delivery and lasts up to 6–9 months [N5-R4][N5-R3]
- Hair gradually returns to normal thickness as hormone levels stabilize [N5-R2][N1-F1]
- Often resolves without specific treatment [N1-F1]

### Abnormal shedding:
- May involve losing **more than four hairs when a doctor gently pulls on the scalp** [N4-R4]
- May be **diffuse and widespread**, not localized or patchy [N4-F2]
- May not improve after several months or may continue for more than six months [N1-F1][N4-R2]
- May be associated with other symptoms such as fatigue, weight changes, or signs of thyroid dysfunction [N4-R1][N4-R3]

If you are losing hair severely, persistently, or in a way that feels out of the ordinary, that is a sign that the shedding may be more than just postpartum telogen effluvium [N4-F2][N1-F1].

## 3) Why postpartum hair shedding happens: the key causes

The evidence points to several key causes, with **hormonal changes** being the main driver.

### Hormone changes
The most important cause is the **postpartum drop in estrogen**, which causes more hair to enter the resting phase and shed [N1-R4][N1-F1][N4-F2]. This is why it is called **telogen effluvium**.

### Stress and other physiological changes
The evidence also points to stress and other postpartum changes as contributing factors [N3-R2][N3-R4]. This is consistent with the general understanding that stress can push more hair into the shedding phase [N3-R2][N3-R4].

### Secondary conditions that can mimic or worsen shedding
The evidence also shows that **thyroid dysfunction** is a common cause of telogen effluvium, especially **hypothyroidism** [N4-R1][N4-R5][N4-F2]. In one study, hypothyroid patients had more severe hair loss than those with normal thyroid function [N4-F2]. This means that if your shedding is severe or does not improve, it is important to consider thyroid function as part of the picture [N4-F2].

## 4) What you can do: safe, evidence-based remedies and treatments

There is **no cure** for postpartum hair loss itself, but there are things you can do to support your hair and reduce further damage [N2-R2][N1-F1]. The safest approach is to combine gentle hair care, good nutrition, and stress management with cautious use of natural remedies [N2-R2][N3-R4].

### Hair care practices that may help
- Use **gentle, sulfate-free shampoos** [N3-R1]
- Avoid harsh brushing, tight hairstyles, and heat styling [N2-R2]
- Consider **scalp massage with natural oils** such as coconut or argan oil, which may improve circulation and nourish hair roots [N3-R1][N2-R1]
- Choose **gentle hair products and hairstyles** to avoid damage [N2-R2]

### Diet and lifestyle tips
- Eat a **balanced diet** with essential nutrients [N3-R1]
- Focus on **good nutrition and stress management**, which are important for overall hair health [N3-R4]
- Get enough **sleep** and manage stress, since stress can worsen shedding [N3-R2][N3-R4]

### Supplements and vitamins
The evidence is more cautious on supplements. The search results say there is **little to no evidence that prenatal vitamins prevent postpartum hair loss** [N6-R4]. That means they are not a proven remedy, though they may support overall health. Other natural ingredients such as **rosemary oil, pumpkin seed oil, and melatonin extract** have been studied for hair growth, but the evidence for them is limited and should be used cautiously [N6-R2][N6-R1].

### What to avoid or be cautious about
- Avoid unproven or over-the-counter products that are not clearly supported by evidence [N6-R4]
- Be cautious about **essential oils and natural remedies**; while they may be used safely, they should be used with care and not relied on as a cure [N6-R1]
- Do not assume that all supplements are safe or effective; evidence is thin for many postpartum hair remedies [N6-R4][N6-R2]

## 5) When to see a doctor or specialist

Postpartum hair shedding usually resolves on its own, but there are clear red flags that suggest an underlying condition and warrant medical attention.

### Red flags that suggest an underlying condition
- Severe or persistent hair loss
- Hair loss that does not improve after several months
- Hair loss that is diffuse and widespread rather than patchy
- Associated symptoms such as fatigue, weight changes, or other signs of thyroid dysfunction [N4-R1][N4-R3][N4-R2][N4-F2]

### Who to see
- First, talk to your **healthcare provider** if you are concerned [N1-F1][N4-R2]
- If thyroid dysfunction is suspected, **thyroid testing** should be part of the workup [N4-F2]
- If the hair loss is severe or persistent, a **dermatologist** may be the most appropriate specialist [N4-F2]

### Next steps if shedding is severe or persistent
- If the shedding continues for more than six months, see a provider [N1-F1]
- If you have other symptoms, get thyroid function testing and other relevant tests [N4-F2]
- If the hair loss does not improve, specialist evaluation is recommended [N4-R2][N4-F2]

## 6) Timeline, prognosis, and realistic expectations

### How long postpartum hair shedding usually lasts
Postpartum hair shedding typically begins within a few months of childbirth, peaks around 4 months after delivery, and lasts up to 6–9 months [N5-R4][N5-R3]. Most women see their hair return to normal thickness about 6–12 months after giving birth [N5-R2][N1-F1].

### Realistic recovery and improvement
- Recovery is gradual, not immediate
- Hair density usually improves over time
- Most women find their hair returns to normal thickness within a **year or two** [N3-R4]
- In the meantime, gentle care, good nutrition, and stress management are recommended [N3-R4]

### When to expect a return to normal hair thickness
- Expect improvement within **6–12 months** [N5-R2][N1-F1]
- Some sources say hair can return to normal thickness within a **year or two** [N3-R4]
- The peak of shedding is around **4 months**, and the loss can last up to **9 months** [N5-R4][N5-R3]

## 7) Bottom line for a patient

If you are asking, “Can you fix postpartum hair shedding?” the short answer is:

- **Yes**, in the sense that it can be supported and managed with the right care.
- **No**, there is no single “magic pill” or instant fix for postpartum telogen effluvium [N2-R2][N1-F1].
- The best approach is to:
  - Understand that it is usually **normal and temporary** [N1-F1][N5-R2]
  - Use **gentle hair care, good nutrition, and stress management** [N2-R2][N3-R4]
  - Avoid unproven supplements and remedies that are not clearly supported by evidence [N6-R4][N6-R1]
  - See a healthcare provider if the shedding is **severe, persistent, or associated with other symptoms** [N1-F1][N4-F2][N4-R2]

In most cases, your hair will gradually return to normal thickness over several months to a year, and the biggest thing you can do is be patient and take care of your overall health [N5-R2][N3-R4].
